A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ARMOR, with v2 extending the work through ARMOR-Think. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated and new content.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety and utility evaluations, test-time scaling, ablations and unseen-strategy experiments in Tables 1–5 and Figures 4–5.

after.justification: v2 retains original ARMOR experiments and adds ARMOR-Think evaluations, a strategy-step training ablation and additional base-model experiments, including Tables 1–3 and 13.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 introduces ARMOR-Think: shortened safety reasoning, separate distilled chain-of-thought reasoning for benign instructions, and preference learning with safety, helpfulness and structure rewards. These change training targets, reward construction and response generation. The original ARMOR pipeline remains.

E1.justification: Utility coverage changes from four MMLU subjects, TruthfulQA and MATH to GSM8k and MATH, removing knowledge and truthfulness evaluations while adding elementary mathematical reasoning. This substantially narrows the kinds of utility assessed. Training instruction sources and safety/jailbreak coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B as an evaluated comparator while retaining the existing main baselines. New Table 13 additionally compares ARMOR adaptations against their unmodified Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B bases. These extend the comparator set without replacing the existing comparison framework.

E3.justification: New settings include ARMOR-Think training with three DPO rounds and about 10k preference pairs per round, a control trained without strategy analysis, and evaluations using 8B and 14B base models. New analyses measure safety-reasoning length and condition safety on intent-extraction correctness. Original attack budgets, judging procedures and decoding settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds intent-extraction analysis (Figure 2), a training ablation testing the necessity of strategy analysis (Table 3), reasoning-length analysis (Figure 5), architecture/scale checks and two ARMOR-Think case studies. It removes three original correlation analyses: strategy-to-safety, intent-to-final-answer and safety-to-final-answer. The other three panels survive in Figure 7.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The additional DPO rounds in v2 describe optimization, not replicated evaluation or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds ARMOR-Think results, including average attack ASR 0.050 and harmfulness 0.009; retained ARMOR values remain 0.060 and 0.002. New utility, ablation, intent, efficiency and base-model results substantially expand the evidence, while MMLU/TruthfulQA results disappear. Retained MATH scores only change rounding. ExHarm SFT prose changes from 0.72 to 0.74 despite retaining the original plot.

T1.justification: Equations 7–8 and Appendix A.5 add the ternary reward definition, safety/helpfulness selection masks and component score vectors. This is a limited formal extension; the original SFT/DPO mathematics is retained, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add ARMOR-Think as a contribution claiming improved utility and reasoning efficiency. They replace the emphasis on human-like structured reasoning with the argument that recovering explicit intent addresses out-of-distribution jailbreaks. The original ARMOR safety and unseen-strategy generalization claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 develops an OOD-to-in-distribution intent explanation and adds the interpretation that policy analysis can correct some erroneous intent extractions. It newly specifies a service threat model excluding attacker access to reasoning and system prompts. Limitations shift from unresolved general-reasoning integration and overhead to residual overhead despite ARMOR-Think.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 documents ARMOR-Think teachers, output formats, training hyperparameters, preference thresholds and per-round data quantities. Tables 8–10 newly disclose the existing ground-truth scoring prompts, and Table 11 supplies the reasoning-refinement prompt. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the original ARMOR settings.

R1.justification: v2 adds the GSM8k reference and three works concerning inference efficiency, while removing the MMLU and TruthfulQA references. The core safety-alignment and jailbreak literature remains substantially the same; the additions provide limited new efficiency context.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, related work is compressed, and analysis paragraphs and headings are recast. Training-format exposition moves into the appendix, while ARMOR-Think and additional-results sections reorganize the narrative. These exceed local wording corrections.

P2.justification: v2 adds intent and reasoning-length plots, ablation and base-model tables, and appendix prompt/example displays. Tables 1–2 are restructured, the correlation figure contracts from six panels to three, and several displays are relocated or compressed. The original framework and data-construction diagrams are retained under new numbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the strategy component through a direct training ablation and improves reproducibility through explicit scoring prompts. ARMOR-Think also provides a tested response to v1’s open reasoning-integration and overhead limitations, with shorter safety reasoning and improved math utility. These gains outweigh the loss of knowledge/truthfulness coverage and the new ExHarm text/figure inconsistency. ARMOR-Think’s higher average benchmark harmfulness remains a material tradeoff alongside the retained original model.
